big-o-cost-you-feel.text: A search endpoint was fine in the demo and fell over at 50k rows. The code did a nested membership scan — O(n^2) — that nobody noticed because it "worked" on 20 test rows. The bug was not a typo; it was a growth rate. This lesson teaches you to read cost as a curve so you catch the O(n^2) before production does.

Big-O is the vocabulary every data-structure choice is argued in. It describes how the number of operations grows as input size n grows, ignoring machine speed and constant factors. That abstraction is exactly what lets you compare a list scan against a set lookup, or a bubble sort against a merge sort, without benchmarking every machine. The whole rest of this course is a catalog of structures indexed by their Big-O for each operation.

big-o-cost-you-feel.prompt: Before reading: algorithm A does 1000*n operations, algorithm B does n*n operations. Which is faster at n=10? At n=100000? What is each ones Big-O?
big-o-cost-you-feel.reveal: At n=10: A does 10000, B does 100 — B wins. At n=100000: A does 10^8, B does 10^10 — A wins by 100x. A is O(n) (the 1000 is a constant, dropped), B is O(n^2). Big-O ignores the constant precisely so it predicts the LARGE-n winner; the small-n crossover is where the constant still matters, and it is real, but it is not what Big-O measures.

big-o-cost-you-feel.code:
def has_dupe_scan(xs):        # O(n^2): for each item, scan the rest
    ops = 0
    for i in range(len(xs)):
        for j in range(i + 1, len(xs)):
            ops += 1
            if xs[i] == xs[j]:
                return True, ops
    return False, ops

def has_dupe_set(xs):          # O(n): one pass, O(1) set membership
    ops = 0
    seen = set()
    for x in xs:
        ops += 1
        if x in seen:
            return True, ops
        seen.add(x)
    return False, ops
big-o-cost-you-feel.intro: Two ways to count duplicates. Instrument both with an operation counter and watch linear beat quadratic as n grows.
steps: The nested loop compares every pair: ~n^2/2 operations, so O(n^2).
The set version touches each element once with an average O(1) membership test: O(n) total.
Big-O drops the 1/2 and the constant — only the n^2 vs n survives, because that is what decides the large-n winner.
Instrumenting op counts makes the growth visible: double n and the scan roughly quadruples while the set roughly doubles.
big-o-cost-you-feel.commonMistake: Calling nested loops "O(n^2)" reflexively even when the inner loop runs a fixed number of times. A loop that always runs 8 times inside an n-loop is O(8n) = O(n); the exponent comes from the inner bound depending on n, not from the nesting itself.

big-o-cost-you-feel.text: Big-O answers one question: as the input size n grows, how does the number of basic operations grow? O(1) means constant — indexing a list, a dict lookup. O(log n) means each step halves the problem — binary search, balanced-tree descent. O(n) means one pass. O(n log n) is the sort barrier for comparison sorts. O(n^2) is every pair — nested scans. O(2^n) is "try every subset" and is intractable past ~30. Two rules make it usable: (1) drop constant factors and lower-order terms — 3n^2 + 5n + 9 is O(n^2), because at large n the n^2 term dominates and the machine speed is a constant; (2) the exponent is the identity of the algorithm and never drops. This is why Big-O predicts the winner at scale even though it says nothing about small inputs: the crossover point where an O(n) with a big constant finally beats an O(n^2) is real, but past it the growth rate wins every time. You will use Big-O to justify every structure choice in this course.

storyboard.say: It starts here: one input of size n. Same data, same request — but two different ways to process it.
One route runs a nested scan — checking every item against every item. That is the O(n squared) path.
The other route makes a single pass and drops results into a set. That is the O(n) path.
On small n, both look fine — the nested scan is a few ops, and the set even pays a little overhead to build.
Now grow n. The nested scan's operations explode as every pair multiplies — the curve bends sharply upward.
The single pass stays linear no matter how big n gets — it never bends, it just extends.
Past the crossover, O(n) wins at scale — the exponent is the algorithm's identity, and a worse constant can never save O(n squared).

arrays-dynamic-arrays.proof: A hand-built dynamic array that tracks size vs capacity, doubles on overflow, and prints exactly when each resize happens over a run of appends.
arrays-dynamic-arrays.unlock: You can explain "amortized O(1)" for append: most appends are O(1), rare ones copy everything, and the average is still constant.
arrays-dynamic-arrays.outcome: Explain why a Python list gives O(1) indexing and amortized O(1) append, and why insert(0)/pop(0) are O(n) — from the dynamic-array mechanism underneath.
arrays-dynamic-arrays.doNotClaim: Don't claim every append is O(1) — a resize append copies all n elements and is O(n); it is the AMORTIZED cost over many appends that is O(1).

arrays-dynamic-arrays.text: A tight loop built a big list with repeated `lst.insert(0, x)` and ran 100x slower than the same loop with `append`. Both look like "add one item," but one shifts every element each time. The difference is the array layout underneath the list. This lesson opens that layout so you predict which operations are cheap.

A Python list is not a linked list — it is a DYNAMIC ARRAY: a contiguous block of pointers plus a size and a (larger) capacity. That contiguity is why lst[i] is O(1) (address = base + i*width) and why insert(0)/pop(0) are O(n) (everything after the gap must shift). Understanding this one mechanism explains most of the list Big-O table you will use for the rest of the course, and it sets up the contrast with linked lists in Module 2.

arrays-dynamic-arrays.prompt: Before reading: a list has size 4 and capacity 4. You append one more item. What must happen, and what does it cost?
arrays-dynamic-arrays.reveal: The backing array is full, so it must GROW: allocate a bigger array, copy all 4 existing pointers into it, then place the new item. That single append is O(n) because of the copy. But growth allocates extra headroom (CPython over-allocates ~1/8 above need), so the next several appends are O(1) with no copy — averaging out to amortized O(1).

arrays-dynamic-arrays.code:
class DynArray:
    def __init__(self):
        self.cap = 1                 # capacity of the backing array
        self.n = 0                   # number of items actually stored
        self.buf = [None] * self.cap
        self.resizes = 0

    def append(self, x):
        if self.n == self.cap:       # full -> grow (this append is O(n))
            self.cap *= 2            # doubling gives amortized O(1)
            new = [None] * self.cap
            for i in range(self.n):  # copy every existing element
                new[i] = self.buf[i]
            self.buf = new
            self.resizes += 1
        self.buf[self.n] = x         # the common case: O(1) write
        self.n += 1
arrays-dynamic-arrays.intro: A dynamic array with explicit size and capacity that doubles when full, logging each resize so the amortization is visible.
steps: size (n) is how many items you have; capacity (cap) is how many slots are allocated.
A normal append writes into a spare slot — O(1).
A full append must allocate a bigger buffer and copy all n items — O(n) — then append.
Doubling capacity means resizes get rarer as the list grows, so the copies amortize to O(1) per append.
arrays-dynamic-arrays.commonMistake: Reaching for insert(0, x) or pop(0) in a loop to build/consume from the front. Each one shifts up to n elements (O(n)), turning the loop into O(n^2); use append/pop() at the end, or a deque (Module 2) for the front.

arrays-dynamic-arrays.text: A Python list stores its elements as a contiguous array of object pointers, together with a size and a capacity where capacity >= size. Contiguity is the whole story for its cost profile. Indexing lst[i] is O(1): the address is base + i * pointer_width, one arithmetic step regardless of n. Appending is amortized O(1): usually there is a spare slot (O(1) write), and when the array fills, CPython allocates a larger buffer (its growth adds roughly 1/8 headroom, following new_allocated = newsize + (newsize>>3) + a small constant) and copies the existing pointers once. Because the extra capacity grows with the list, the O(n) copies happen geometrically less often, so averaged over many appends the cost per append is constant — that is what "amortized O(1)" means. The flip side: inserting or deleting anywhere but the end must shift every following element to keep the block contiguous, so insert(0)/pop(0)/remove are O(n). This dynamic-array mechanism is the baseline every other linear structure is compared against.
arrays-dynamic-arrays.title: A list is a dynamic array: contiguity buys O(1) index, and growth is amortized

storyboard.say: It starts with append(x): you hand one element to the list and ask it to tack that value onto the end.
First the list checks capacity: is the used size already equal to the total slots the buffer holds?
If there is room, it takes the fast path and writes x straight into the next spare slot, an O(1) move.
That write just stores a pointer into the contiguous buffer, no shifting, no reallocation needed.
But if the buffer is full, the list must first allocate a bigger buffer to make space, an O(n) detour.
Growing copies every existing pointer into the new block and replaces the old buffer with it.
The key insight: extra capacity grows with the list, so those O(n) copies get rarer, making append amortized O(1).

memory-cache-contiguity.doNotClaim: Don't claim Big-O is the whole cost story — two O(n) scans can differ by an order of magnitude in wall-clock time purely from memory layout and cache behavior.

memory-cache-contiguity.text: Two engineers implemented the same O(n) aggregation. One used a flat list of numbers, the other a list of small objects scattered across the heap. Same Big-O, but the flat version ran 8x faster. The reason was not the algorithm — it was the memory hierarchy. This lesson explains the layer Big-O hides so your "equal" choices are not secretly unequal.

Big-O counts operations as if every memory access costs the same. Real CPUs do not: reading from cache is ~1ns, reading from main memory is ~100ns, and the CPU pulls memory in fixed-size CACHE LINES (commonly 64 bytes). Structures that store data CONTIGUOUSLY (arrays) let one line load serve many elements; structures that scatter data (linked lists, trees of heap objects) force a fresh, slow load per element. This is why the array in the last lesson is not just O(1)-index good but also cache-good, and it frames every array-vs-pointer tradeoff ahead.

memory-cache-contiguity.prompt: Before reading: two programs sum 1,000,000 integers, both O(n). One reads them from a contiguous array, one from a linked list of scattered nodes. Why can the linked-list one be many times slower?
memory-cache-contiguity.reveal: Cache lines. The array stores integers back-to-back, so one 64-byte line load brings in several at once (spatial locality) and the CPU prefetches ahead — most accesses hit cache. The linked list stores nodes wherever the allocator put them, so each `node.next` jumps to an unpredictable address, likely a cache MISS costing ~100x a hit. Same operation count, very different memory-stall count.

memory-cache-contiguity.intro: Model the memory hierarchy: walking contiguous data loads one cache line per BLOCK of elements; pointer-chasing loads a line per element.
steps: A cache line holds several contiguous elements; one load serves all of them.
A sequential array walk pays one line load per LINE elements — the rest are cache hits.
Pointer chasing jumps to scattered addresses, so each element tends to be its own line load (a miss).
Same n and same Big-O, but ~n/LINE loads vs ~n loads — the constant the hardware charges is very different.
memory-cache-contiguity.commonMistake: Assuming a "list of objects" and a "list of numbers" scan at the same speed because both are O(n). A list of objects stores pointers to scattered heap objects, so touching each object field is a likely cache miss; a flat array of numbers is contiguous and stays hot in cache.

memory-cache-contiguity.text: CPUs read memory in fixed-size cache lines (often 64 bytes) into small, fast caches. Two properties decide whether your accesses hit that fast cache. SPATIAL LOCALITY: if you use data near data you just used, it is probably already in the loaded line — so a sequential walk over a contiguous array gets many elements per line load, and hardware prefetchers race ahead to hide the latency. TEMPORAL LOCALITY: reusing the same data soon keeps it hot. A contiguous array (Python list of numbers, or any packed buffer) has excellent spatial locality; a pointer-linked structure (linked list, or a list of heap objects) does not, because `next`/field accesses jump to addresses the allocator scattered, each a likely cache MISS that stalls the CPU ~100x longer than a hit. This is why two O(n) scans can differ 10x: Big-O counts operations, the memory hierarchy counts line loads, and the line-load count is dominated by layout. The practical rule: prefer contiguous layouts for data you scan hot; reach for pointer structures only when you need their algorithmic wins (O(1) splice, ordered traversal) enough to pay the locality tax.

storyboard.say: The CPU never touches memory directly. Every read it issues first asks the small, fast cache to serve the data.
Hardware never fetches one byte. It pulls a whole 64-byte cache line at once, betting you'll want the neighbors too.
Walk a contiguous array and that single line already holds many elements, so the next reads are cache hits at about one nanosecond.
When the data you want isn't in cache, you take a miss and pay roughly a hundred nanoseconds to fetch a fresh line from slow main memory.
Scattered heap nodes live at addresses the allocator flung apart, so each pointer hop lands off-line and forces its own slow fetch.
Same Big-O, wildly different reality: the array amortizes one load across many elements while the pointer chase pays full latency per node.
That's the layer Big-O hides. Contiguity plus locality is why the flat list ran eight times faster on identical work.

amortized-analysis.doNotClaim: Don't claim amortized O(1) means every operation is O(1) — it means the TOTAL over n operations is O(n), so the average is O(1); a single operation can still be O(n).

amortized-analysis.text: A code reviewer flagged your dynamic-array append as "O(n) worst case, so this loop is O(n^2)." That is the wrong analysis — and shipping a slower "fix" to satisfy it would be worse. Amortized analysis is the tool that proves the loop is actually O(n). This lesson gives you the argument so you can defend the right design with numbers.

Amortized analysis measures the average cost of an operation over a WORST-CASE SEQUENCE, not the worst case of a single operation. It is the honest way to cost data structures whose operations are usually cheap but occasionally expensive: dynamic-array append, hash-table resize, splay-tree access. Without it you would over-pessimistically call append O(n) and mis-design around a spike that averages away. This closes Module 1 by turning the "amortized O(1)" you have been using into something you can prove.

amortized-analysis.prompt: Before reading: appending n items to a doubling array triggers resizes that copy 1, 2, 4, 8, ... elements. What is the TOTAL copy work across all resizes, and the average per append?
amortized-analysis.reveal: The copies sum to 1 + 2 + 4 + ... + n/2 < n (a geometric series that totals less than n). Add the n cheap O(1) writes and total work is < 2n = O(n). Divided over n appends, that is O(1) amortized per append. The key is the geometric series: each resize is twice as expensive but happens half as often, so the whole sequence stays linear.

amortized-analysis.code:
def append_costs(n):
    cap, size = 1, 0
    total = 0
    for _ in range(n):
        if size == cap:          # resize: copy 'size' existing elements
            total += size        # the O(size) copy cost of this append
            cap *= 2
        total += 1               # the O(1) write every append pays
        size += 1
    return total                 # aggregate cost of the whole sequence

# amortized cost = total / n  -> a small constant, not n
amortized-analysis.intro: The aggregate method: sum the real cost of every append over a doubling run, then divide by the number of appends.
steps: Every append pays 1 for the write; that alone is n across the sequence.
Resizes add copy costs 1, 2, 4, ... — a geometric series summing to < n total.
Aggregate cost is therefore < 2n = O(n) for n appends.
Amortized cost = O(n) / n = O(1); the O(n) spikes are real but averaged away.
amortized-analysis.commonMistake: Confusing amortized with average-case over random inputs. Amortized is a guarantee over ANY sequence of operations (worst-case sequence), with no probability assumption; average-case makes assumptions about input distribution. They are different claims.

amortized-analysis.text: A single dynamic-array append is O(n) in the worst case (the one that triggers a resize copies all elements). Naively that suggests a loop of n appends is O(n^2). Amortized analysis proves it is actually O(n). The AGGREGATE METHOD sums the true cost of the whole sequence and divides by the count. For doubling growth: the writes cost n total, and the resize copies cost 1 + 2 + 4 + ... + n/2, a geometric series that sums to less than n. Total < 2n, so the amortized cost per append is < 2 = O(1). The load-bearing fact is that geometric growth (double, or CPython's ~1.125x factor) makes each resize twice as costly but half as frequent, keeping the series bounded. Contrast constant growth — grow by a FIXED 10 slots each time: then resizes at size 10, 20, 30, ... copy 10 + 20 + 30 + ... ~ n^2/20 total, which is O(n) amortized per append and O(n^2) for the loop. That is why real dynamic arrays multiply capacity rather than add to it. Amortized O(1) means the sequence total is O(n); it never claims each individual operation is O(1).

storyboard.say: We run n appends onto a dynamic array — this is the sequence a reviewer wrongly costed at O(n squared).
Most appends are cheap: each one just writes a single element into open space, paying exactly one.
Rarely an append is full and must resize, copying every existing element — an O(n) spike.
Aggregate the real work: the writes contribute n total across the whole run.
Now the copies. Doubling makes each resize twice as costly but half as often: 1+2+4+…+n/2, a geometric series under n.
Everything lands in one aggregate: total work is less than 2n, not the feared n squared.
Divide that bounded total by n appends and each one amortizes to under two — constant, O(1). The reviewer was wrong.

For hard real-time or tail-latency-sensitive paths, the O(n) resize spike is unacceptable even though the average is fine; pre-allocate or use a bounded structure (B). Amortized is a promise about totals, not about any single operations latency.

linked-lists.proof: A linked list that inserts three values at the head and prints the computed traversal order, demonstrating O(1) head insertion.
linked-lists.unlock: You can explain why a linked list gives O(1) head insertion but O(n) indexing, the mirror image of an array.
linked-lists.outcome: Build a singly linked list from nodes, traverse it, and insert at the head in O(1) — then explain the exact tradeoff it makes against an array.
linked-lists.doNotClaim: Don't claim linked lists are "faster than arrays" — they trade O(1) index for O(1) splicing and pay a cache-locality tax; each is faster only for its own access pattern.

linked-lists.text: A team kept an ordered log in a Python list and used insert(0, x) to prepend the newest entry — O(n) every write, quadratic under load. A linked list prepends in O(1). But before you reach for one, you must know what you give up: random access. This lesson builds the structure so the tradeoff is concrete, not folklore.

A linked list stores each element in its own NODE that holds a value and a reference to the next node. There is no contiguous block, so there is no address arithmetic: you cannot jump to index i, you must walk from the head. In exchange, splicing a node in or out is O(1) once you hold the neighbor — no shifting. Linked lists underlie deques, adjacency lists, LRU caches, and undo stacks, and they are the canonical foil to the array from Module 1.

linked-lists.prompt: Before reading: in a singly linked list, how do you get the 5th element, and how do you add a new first element? Which is cheap, which is not?
linked-lists.reveal: To get the 5th element you must start at the head and follow `.next` four times — O(n), because there is no index arithmetic. To add a new first element you make a node whose `.next` points at the current head, then move head to it — O(1), no shifting. That is the exact inverse of an array, which has O(1) index but O(n) front insertion.

linked-lists.intro: A node holds a value and a next pointer. Prepend by pointing the new node at the old head; traverse by following next until None.
steps: Each Node owns a value and a reference to the next Node (or None at the tail).
push_front builds a node whose next is the current head, then updates head — O(1).
Because we prepend, the traversal order is the reverse of insertion order.
to_list walks head -> next -> next until None; that walk is O(n) and there is no shortcut to index i.
linked-lists.commonMistake: Losing the rest of the list by setting head to the new node BEFORE linking the new node to the old head. You must capture `new.next = self.head` first, then move head — otherwise the old chain is orphaned and lost.

linked-lists.text: A linked list is a chain of nodes; each node stores a value and a pointer to the next node, with the last node pointing at None. Because nodes are separate heap allocations rather than one contiguous block, the list gives up the arrays superpower — you cannot compute the address of element i, so indexing and search are O(n) walks from the head. What you get back is O(1) STRUCTURAL EDITS: to insert at the head you allocate a node and repoint two references; to delete or splice in the middle you rewire a couple of `next` pointers, with NO shifting of other elements. (A doubly linked list adds a `prev` pointer so you can also delete a node in O(1) given only that node, at the cost of an extra pointer per node.) The hidden cost, from the memory lesson, is locality: nodes scattered across the heap defeat the cache, so even an O(n) linked-list scan is typically slower than an O(n) array scan. The decision rule that falls out: choose a linked list when your workload is dominated by insertions/deletions at known positions (queues, LRU eviction, adjacency lists) and choose an array when you index, scan, or append at the end.
linked-lists.title: A linked list trades address arithmetic for O(1) splicing

storyboard.say: The trigger: we want to add the newest entry to the front of the list, so we allocate a fresh node to hold that value.
The head pointer marks the front of the chain. To prepend, we make head point at our new node — a single O(1) reference swap.
The new node's next pointer now aims at the old front, node A, splicing it into the chain with no shifting of any element.
The rest of the chain is untouched: node A still links to node B along its next pointer, exactly as before.
The final node points at None, marking the tail — this sentinel is how a walk knows it has reached the end.
The tradeoff: there is no address arithmetic, so to reach index i you must walk next from head — O(n) traversal.
The core insight: you trade random access for O(1) structural edits — insertion is just repointing two references at the head.

    out = []
    # follow next_index from head until -1
    return out

def reverse_links(nodes, head):

nodes = [[10, 1], [20, 2], [30, 3], [40, -1]]
head = 0

If you locate positions by index and mostly read/scan, the array (B) wins on both indexing and locality. The deciding question is whether you arrive at the edit point via a reference or via an index.

In return, inserting/deleting at the head or a held position is O(1) with no shifting. It is the mirror image of the arrays cost profile, plus a cache-locality penalty from scattered nodes.

stacks.proof: A bracket-matching checker built on a stack that prints balanced/unbalanced verdicts computed from actual push/pop operations.
stacks.unlock: You can explain LIFO and name the class of problems (nesting, backtracking, undo) that a stack solves naturally.
stacks.outcome: Implement a stack with O(1) push/pop and use its LIFO order to solve a real problem: matching nested brackets.
stacks.doNotClaim: Don't claim a stack is "just a list" — its VALUE is the LIFO discipline that makes nesting and reversal problems trivial; the restriction is the feature.

stacks.text: A parser accepted `([)]` as valid because it only counted brackets instead of tracking their nesting order. Counting cannot catch interleaving; a stack can, because the last opener must be the first to close. This lesson builds the stack and uses its LIFO order to make the bug impossible.

A stack is a last-in, first-out (LIFO) collection with two O(1) operations: push (add to top) and pop (remove the top). You already have the mechanism — a Python list append/pop is a stack — but the POINT is the discipline: LIFO exactly models nested and reversible processes. Function call frames, expression evaluation, depth-first search, browser back, and undo all ride on a stack. This lesson is also the setup for DFS in Module 5, which is a stack walk.

stacks.prompt: Before reading: why can a stack validate `([{}])` but a simple counter of "opens minus closes" cannot?
stacks.reveal: A counter only checks that the NUMBER of opens equals closes; it accepts `([)]` because the counts balance. A stack checks ORDER: each closer must match the most recent unmatched opener (the top of the stack). When you see `)` the top must be `(`; in `([)]` the top is `[`, so it fails. LIFO enforces correct nesting, which counting cannot.

stacks.intro: Push every opening bracket; on a closing bracket, the top of the stack must be its matching opener, else the string is unbalanced.
steps: Every opening bracket is pushed onto the stack (O(1) append).
A closing bracket must match the top of the stack — pop and compare (O(1)).
A mismatch, or a closer with an empty stack, means the nesting is wrong.
A non-empty stack at the end means unclosed openers remain — also unbalanced.
stacks.commonMistake: Popping without first checking the stack is non-empty. A string that starts with a closing bracket (like `)`) pops an empty stack; guard with `if not stack` before comparing, or you crash on valid-looking-but-unbalanced input.

stacks.text: A stack exposes exactly two O(1) operations plus a peek: push adds to the TOP, pop removes and returns the TOP, and peek reads the top without removing it. The defining property is LIFO — last in, first out — and that single constraint is the whole value. Any process where the most recently opened thing must close first is a stack: matching brackets and tags, evaluating expressions (operators/operands), the call stack of function invocations, depth-first traversal, and undo/redo histories. In Python a plain list IS a stack: append is push and pop() is pop, both amortized O(1) at the end (never pop(0), which is O(n)). The reason to name it a stack rather than "a list" is intent and correctness: by restricting yourself to top-only access you get an invariant — the element you remove is always the newest unmatched one — that directly solves nesting and reversal without extra bookkeeping. The bracket checker is the archetype: counting brackets fails on interleaving like `([)]` because it ignores order, while the stack captures order for free. When you see nesting, backtracking, or "reverse this," reach for a stack.
stacks.title: A stack is LIFO discipline, and the restriction is what makes nesting easy

storyboard.say: A parser wrongly accepted the interleaved string bracket-paren-close-bracket-close because it only counted brackets. Let's fix that by scanning character by character.
For each character we classify it: is this an opening bracket, or a closing one? That single decision routes everything.
If it's an opener, we push it onto the stack, recording that a nested context just began.
Push adds to the TOP of the stack, so the newest opener always sits on top, ready to be closed first. That's LIFO.
If instead it's a closer, we don't count; we peek and pop the top opener to see what we're actually closing.
The closer must match that top opener. If it mismatches, or the stack is empty, the string is unbalanced.
This is why counting fails but a stack wins: LIFO enforces nesting order, so bracket-paren-close-bracket-close is rejected the moment close-bracket meets an open paren on top.

stacks.summary: The worked example used a stack to check balance (a yes/no). Here you use the same stack to compute the MAXIMUM nesting depth, and return -1 for malformed input — a richer answer the balance check throws away.

optionA.text: append/pop at the end are amortized O(1) and the code is idiomatic. Ideal for a single-threaded stack; the only caveat is never using pop(0)/insert(0).
optionA.label: Plain list

optionB.text: deque also does append/pop in O(1) and adds thread-safe atomic operations. Slightly more overhead and less common for a pure stack, but safer under concurrent access.
optionB.label: deque as a stack

stacks.guidance: For an ordinary single-threaded stack, a list (A) is the idiomatic, fast choice — push=append, pop=pop(). Use a deque (B) when multiple threads share the stack and you want atomic append/pop, or when you also need O(1) operations at the FRONT (then it is really a deque, next lesson). Do not reach for deque just to "have a stack."

The stack enforces ORDER: each closer must match the most recent opener on top, so `([)]` fails, while a counter only checks totals.

stacks.question: Why does a stack correctly reject `([)]` while a counter of opens vs closes accepts it?

queues-deques.proof: A FIFO queue on collections.deque that enqueues and dequeues a sequence and prints the computed service order plus what remains.
queues-deques.unlock: You can explain FIFO vs LIFO and why deque gives O(1) at BOTH ends where a list gives O(1) at only one.
queues-deques.outcome: Implement a FIFO queue with O(1) enqueue and dequeue using a deque, and explain why a plain list makes dequeue O(n).
queues-deques.doNotClaim: Don't claim a Python list is a fine queue — list.pop(0) is O(n) because it shifts every element, so a list-backed queue is secretly O(n^2) under load.

queues-deques.text: A task worker used a list with pop(0) to pull the next job FIFO. It passed tests and then melted under a backlog: every dequeue shifted the whole list. The fix is a deque, which pops the front in O(1). This lesson builds the correct FIFO queue and shows exactly where the list version goes quadratic.

A queue is first-in, first-out (FIFO): items leave in the order they arrived — the fairness model for job schedulers, request buffers, and BFS. A deque (double-ended queue) generalizes it: O(1) push and pop at BOTH ends, so it serves as a queue, a stack, or a sliding window. In Python, collections.deque is the right tool: append/appendleft/pop/popleft are all ~O(1), whereas a list is O(1) only at the end. This lesson pairs with the stack (LIFO) to complete the linear-access family and directly powers BFS in Module 5.

queues-deques.prompt: Before reading: you implement a queue with a Python list, enqueue with append and dequeue with pop(0). What is the cost of dequeue, and why?
queues-deques.reveal: pop(0) is O(n): removing the first element leaves a hole at index 0, so every remaining element must shift down one slot to keep the array contiguous. Do that for each of n dequeues and the whole drain is O(n^2). A deque avoids this because popleft() removes from the front without shifting a contiguous block.

queues-deques.intro: Use a deque: append to enqueue at the back, popleft to dequeue from the front — both O(1) — preserving arrival order.
steps: enqueue appends to the RIGHT (back) of the deque — O(1).
dequeue pops from the LEFT (front) — O(1) — returning the oldest item (FIFO).
Arrival order is preserved: the first enqueued is the first dequeued.
A deque supports both ends in O(1); that is why it beats a list, which is O(1) only at the back.
queues-deques.commonMistake: Using a list with pop(0) for a queue "because it works." It works correctly but is O(n) per dequeue, so a busy queue becomes O(n^2). Reach for collections.deque, whose popleft is O(1).

queues-deques.text: A queue is FIFO: elements are served in arrival order, which is the fairness guarantee behind job schedulers, message buffers, rate limiters, and breadth-first search. The operations are enqueue (add at the back) and dequeue (remove from the front). The subtlety is cost at the FRONT. A dynamic array (Python list) is O(1) at the back but O(n) at the front, because removing index 0 forces every later element to shift down to keep memory contiguous — so a list-backed queue silently becomes O(n^2) as it drains. collections.deque is implemented as a doubly linked list of fixed-size blocks, giving approximately O(1) append and pop at BOTH ends (append, appendleft, pop, popleft); it trades away O(1) random indexing (deque indexing is O(n) in the middle) to get cheap ends. A DEQUE generalizes both a queue and a stack: use one end for LIFO, both ends for FIFO or a sliding window. The rule: for anything that adds and removes at opposite ends, or at the front at all, use a deque; keep a list when you only append and index at the end.
queues-deques.title: FIFO fairness needs O(1) at both ends, which a deque provides and a list does not
FIFO queue on a deque

storyboard.say: A queue is first-in, first-out: jobs arrive at the enqueue entry and must leave in the exact order they came in.
Enqueue adds the newest job at the back of the buffer with append, which is a cheap O(1) tail operation.
The deque buffer holds jobs in arrival order, so the oldest one always sits waiting at the front.
Dequeue serves that oldest job by popping the front, and the worker hands it off to be processed.
Here is the trap: a Python list pops the back in O(1) but pop(0) at the front shifts every element down.
Under a backlog that per-dequeue shift makes a list-backed queue silently go quadratic as it drains.
collections.deque is a linked list of blocks, so append and popleft are both O(1) and the whole flow stays fast.

list-vs-linked-decision.proof: A cost model that tallies the total Big-O work of a given operation mix for both a list and a linked list and prints which structure wins.

list-vs-linked-decision.text: A design review stalled on "list or linked list?" with both sides quoting Big-O tables at each other. The answer is not in the table alone — it is in which operations this workload actually does and how often. This lesson turns that argument into a computation you can settle with numbers.

This lesson closes Module 2 by making the array-vs-linked decision explicit. Every structure so far has a per-operation cost profile: arrays are O(1) index and end-append but O(n) front/middle edits; linked lists are O(1) known-position splice but O(n) index/search, with worse locality. The right choice depends on the WORKLOAD — the frequencies of index, search, append, front-insert, middle-splice. You will build a tiny cost model that scores a workload against both, which is the reusable method for the choosing lessons in Module 5.

list-vs-linked-decision.prompt: Before reading: workload X is 90% random indexing, 10% end-append. Workload Y is 90% front-insertion, 10% sequential scan. Which structure fits each?
list-vs-linked-decision.reveal: X (mostly random index + end append) fits an ARRAY: O(1) index and amortized O(1) append, and its scans are cache-friendly — a linked list would make the 90% indexing O(n). Y (mostly front-insertion) fits a LINKED LIST / deque: O(1) front insert vs the arrays O(n) shift. The operation MIX, weighted by frequency, decides — not a blanket preference.

list-vs-linked-decision.code:
# cost[op] = (list_cost, linked_cost) as a growth class: 1 == O(1), N == O(n)
N = 1000  # stand-in for n when an op is O(n)
COST = {
    "index":        (1, N),   # array: address math; linked: walk
    "append_end":   (1, 1),   # both O(1) (linked with a tail pointer)
    "insert_front": (N, 1),   # array shifts; linked repoints
    "search":       (N, N),   # both scan
}

def score(workload):
    list_total = sum(freq * COST[op][0] for op, freq in workload.items())
    linked_total = sum(freq * COST[op][1] for op, freq in workload.items())
    return list_total, linked_total
list-vs-linked-decision.intro: Assign each operation its Big-O cost class (1 or n) per structure, weight by how often the workload does it, and sum to a comparable score.
steps: Model each op as O(1) (=1) or O(n) (=N) for each structure — the growth class is what matters.
Multiply each ops cost by how many times the workload performs it.
Sum per structure to get a total work score in the same units.
The lower score wins; the winner changes when you change the frequencies.
list-vs-linked-decision.commonMistake: Choosing by a single "headline" operation ("linked lists have O(1) insert!") while ignoring that the workload spends 90% of its time indexing, where the linked list is O(n). Weight by FREQUENCY, not by the most memorable feature.

list-vs-linked-decision.text: There is no universally best linear structure — only a best fit for a workload. Make the choice a computation. First, list the operations your code actually performs and their frequencies (index, search, append-end, insert-front, splice-middle, iterate). Second, look up each operations growth class for each candidate: a Python list is O(1) index, amortized O(1) end-append, O(n) front/middle insert, O(n) search, with excellent cache locality on scans; a linked list is O(1) known-position splice and O(1) head/tail insert (with tail pointer), but O(n) index and search and poor locality. Third, weight each cost by its frequency and sum — the structure with the lower weighted total wins. This exposes why the answer flips: an index-heavy workload favors the array even though the linked list "has O(1) insert," and an insert-at-known-position workload favors the linked list even though the array "has O(1) index." Big-O tables are inputs to this decision, not the decision; the frequencies are what turn a table into a choice. Locality is a tiebreaker: when two options tie on growth class, the contiguous one is usually faster in practice.

Now the two totals face off head to head — the comparison the Big-O table alone could never resolve.

hash-maps.proof: A chaining hash map that inserts several keys, prints which bucket each landed in, and returns computed lookups — including a deliberately collided pair.
hash-maps.unlock: You can explain the hash -> bucket -> compare-key mechanism and why the O(1) is an AVERAGE, not a guarantee.
hash-maps.outcome: Implement a hash map from scratch — hash to a bucket, store key/value pairs, resolve collisions by chaining — and explain why lookup is average O(1) but worst-case O(n).
hash-maps.doNotClaim: Don't claim dict lookups are "always O(1)" — that is the AVERAGE with a good hash and bounded load factor; adversarial or degenerate hashes push a bucket to O(n).

hash-maps.text: A service assumed dict access was free and put a hot lookup in its inner loop. Fine — until a batch of keys that all hashed into one bucket turned that "O(1)" into an O(n) chain walk and latency spiked. Understanding what a hash map really does under the hood is how you keep the average case average. This lesson builds one so the caveats are visible.

A hash map (Python dict) is the workhorse of practical programming: near-constant-time insert, lookup, and delete by key. It works by HASHING a key to an integer, mapping that to a bucket index, and storing the key/value there. Because different keys can map to the same bucket (a collision), a real hash map needs a resolution strategy — chaining (a list per bucket) or open addressing (probe to another slot). This lesson builds a chaining map to expose the mechanism; the collision and load-factor details come in the next lessons.

hash-maps.prompt: Before reading: two different keys hash to the same bucket. How does a hash map still return the right value for each, and what does that do to lookup cost for those keys?
hash-maps.reveal: It stores the full KEY alongside each value, and on lookup it scans that bucket comparing keys with == until it finds the matching one. So collided keys share a bucket but stay distinguishable. The cost: a lookup in a bucket holding k entries is O(k). With a good hash and a bounded load factor, k is ~1 on average (O(1)); if many keys collide, k grows and lookup degrades toward O(n).

hash-maps.intro: Hash the key, mod by the number of buckets to get an index, and store (key, value) in that buckets list; look up by scanning only that bucket.
steps: hash(key) turns the key into an integer; % nbuckets maps it to a bucket index.
put scans the target bucket to update an existing key, else appends the pair (chaining).
get scans ONLY the target bucket, comparing keys with == — not the whole map.
With ~1 entry per bucket, that scan is O(1) average; a crowded bucket makes it O(chain length).
hash-maps.commonMistake: Storing only values, keyed by bucket index, and forgetting to keep the KEY. Then two colliding keys are indistinguishable and get returns the wrong value. A hash map must store and compare the full key, because the bucket index is lossy.

hash-maps.text: A hash map answers "what value is stored under this key?" in average constant time. The mechanism has three steps: (1) compute hash(key), an integer derived from the keys contents; (2) reduce it to a bucket index, e.g. hash % number_of_buckets; (3) within that bucket, store or find the entry by comparing the full key with ==. Step 3 is why keys are stored, not just values: the hash and the index are LOSSY (many keys share a bucket), so equality on the key is what makes the answer exact. Collisions — distinct keys landing in the same bucket — are unavoidable (pigeonhole), so the map needs a resolution scheme; here it is CHAINING: each bucket holds a list of entries, and you scan that short list. The cost of any operation is therefore proportional to the length of ONE bucket. With a good hash function (spreads keys uniformly) and a bounded LOAD FACTOR (entries / buckets kept small, e.g. under ~0.66 for CPythons dict), the average bucket holds ~1 entry, giving average O(1) insert/get/delete. The WORST case is O(n): if every key hashes to the same bucket, one chain holds them all and you are back to a linear scan. So "dict is O(1)" is an average that depends on the hash quality and the load factor — the very things the next two lessons control.

sets-dedup.proof: A dedup-preserving-order function and set algebra (intersection/union) whose computed results are printed from real set operations.
sets-dedup.unlock: You can explain why set membership is average O(1) and why only HASHABLE values can be members.

sets-dedup.text: A pipeline deduped records with `if x not in result: result.append(x)` over a list — an O(n^2) trap that crawled on big inputs (you saw its shape in Lesson 1). A set makes membership average O(1) and the whole dedup O(n). This lesson shows the set as a specialized hash map and the constraint that comes with it.

A set is a hash map that stores keys with no values: it answers "is x present?" in average O(1) and automatically holds each element at most once. That makes it the tool for membership tests, deduplication, and set algebra (union, intersection, difference). Because it is hash-based, its members must be HASHABLE — their hash must be stable, which in Python means immutable-identity types (numbers, strings, tuples of hashables), not lists or dicts. Sets recur everywhere: visited-tracking in graph search (Module 5), dedup, and fast "is this allowed?" checks.

sets-dedup.prompt: Before reading: why is `x in some_set` average O(1) but `x in some_list` O(n)? And why can you not put a list into a set?
sets-dedup.reveal: A set hashes x to a bucket and checks just that bucket — average O(1), same mechanism as a dict. A list has no such index into its contents, so `in` scans every element — O(n). You cannot add a list to a set because a list is mutable: its contents (and thus its hash) could change after insertion, which would misplace it in the table and break lookups — so Python forbids unhashable members and raises TypeError.

sets-dedup.intro: Dedup while preserving first-seen order using a set as the "seen" tracker, and compute set algebra directly.
steps: A set gives average O(1) membership, so "have I seen x?" is constant, not a list scan.
Adding x to the set marks it seen; the output list preserves first-seen order the set does not track.
Set algebra is built in: & is intersection, | is union, - is difference.
Only hashable values can be members; that is the price of the O(1) lookup.
sets-dedup.commonMistake: Relying on set iteration order for anything meaningful. Sets are UNORDERED — iteration order is an implementation detail and must not be depended on. If you need order (like first-seen dedup), track it separately in a list as shown.

sets-dedup.text: A set is a hash table that stores only keys, so it answers membership ("is x in the set?") in average O(1) by the same hash -> bucket -> compare mechanism as a dict, and it stores each distinct element at most once. That gives three superpowers. MEMBERSHIP: replacing `x in list` (O(n)) with `x in set` (average O(1)) collapses the classic O(n^2) "seen it?" loop to O(n) — the single most common real-world use. DEDUP: `set(iterable)` removes duplicates in O(n); wrap with an order-preserving pass if order matters, since a set itself is UNORDERED. SET ALGEBRA: intersection (&), union (|), difference (-), and subset tests run over the hash tables, roughly O(len) rather than nested scans. The constraint is HASHABILITY: members must have a stable hash, which in Python means immutable-identity types (int, str, tuple of hashables, frozenset). Mutable containers (list, dict, set) are unhashable because their contents could change after insertion, which would silently misplace them and corrupt lookups — so adding one raises TypeError. The mental model: reach for a set whenever the question is "is it present / is it unique," and reach for a dict when you also need an associated value.

collisions-load-factor.proof: A hash table that tracks its load factor and rehashes into a bigger table when it crosses a threshold, printing average chain length before and after.
collisions-load-factor.unlock: You can define load factor (n/buckets), explain why it drives cost, and describe what a resize/rehash does.
collisions-load-factor.outcome: Explain the two collision-resolution strategies (chaining vs open addressing), define load factor, and show why exceeding a threshold triggers a resize that keeps operations O(1).
collisions-load-factor.doNotClaim: Don't claim more buckets is always better — an over-sized table wastes memory and hurts cache locality; the goal is a bounded load factor, not the largest table.

collisions-load-factor.text: A cache built on a fixed-size hash table got slower as it filled: with too few buckets, every bucket became a long chain and "O(1)" lookups crawled. The missing piece was resizing on load factor. This lesson makes load factor a number you monitor and act on, so the average case stays average.

Collisions are inescapable — by the pigeonhole principle, more keys than buckets guarantees sharing — so every hash table needs a resolution strategy and a growth policy. The two strategies are CHAINING (a list per bucket) and OPEN ADDRESSING (probe to the next slot on collision, what CPythons dict uses). The dial that controls performance is the LOAD FACTOR = entries / buckets: as it rises, chains lengthen / probe sequences grow and operations drift from O(1) toward O(n). Real tables RESIZE when the load factor crosses a threshold (CPython keeps its dict at most ~2/3 full). This lesson makes that mechanism concrete.

collisions-load-factor.prompt: Before reading: a hash table has 4 buckets and you insert 40 keys. What is the load factor, roughly how long is each chain, and what should the table do about it?
collisions-load-factor.reveal: Load factor = 40/4 = 10, so with a good hash each bucket holds ~10 entries and every lookup scans ~10 — an order of magnitude off the O(1) ideal. The table should RESIZE: allocate many more buckets and rehash all entries into them, dropping the load factor back below the threshold (~0.66) so chains return to ~1 and lookups return to O(1).

collisions-load-factor.intro: Track load factor as entries/buckets; when it exceeds a threshold, allocate a bigger table and rehash every entry into it.
steps: Load factor = entries / buckets measures how crowded the table is.
Rising load factor means longer chains (or probe sequences), pushing cost toward O(n).
When load factor crosses the threshold, allocate a bigger table and REHASH every entry (indices change with the new bucket count).
After the resize the load factor drops and average chain length returns to ~1, restoring O(1).
collisions-load-factor.commonMistake: Resizing but reusing the old bucket indices without rehashing. Bucket index depends on `hash(key) % nbuckets`, and nbuckets changed — every entry must be re-placed with the NEW modulus, or lookups will look in the wrong bucket and miss.

collisions-load-factor.text: Collisions are guaranteed (pigeonhole: n keys into m<n buckets forces sharing), so a hash table is defined by two choices. RESOLUTION: chaining stores a list per bucket and scans it; open addressing stores entries directly in the table and, on collision, PROBES to another slot by a rule (linear probing steps to the next slot; the cost of a lookup is the length of the probe sequence). CPythons dict uses open addressing. GROWTH: the LOAD FACTOR = number_of_entries / number_of_buckets is the single number that predicts performance — at load factor around 0.5-0.66 the average bucket/probe is short and operations are O(1); as it approaches 1 (and beyond, for chaining) collisions pile up and cost drifts toward O(n). So real tables set a THRESHOLD and RESIZE when crossed: allocate a larger table (geometric growth) and REHASH every existing entry into it, because each entrys bucket is hash(key) % new_bucket_count and that count changed. CPython keeps its dict at most ~2/3 full for this reason. The resize is O(n) but amortizes away (same geometric argument as dynamic arrays), and it is what preserves the average O(1) the whole structure is sold on. More buckets is not free: an over-large table wastes memory and hurts locality, so the target is a BOUNDED load factor, not a maximal table.
collisions-load-factor.title: Load factor drives cost; resizing keeps it bounded so operations stay O(1)

collisions-load-factor.subtitle: crossing the threshold triggers grow + rehash, restoring short chains

storyboard.say: Every insert lands here: we add the entry and bump n, the running count of items in the table.
Because n changed, we recompute the load factor — entries divided by buckets — and check it against the threshold.
If it's below the threshold, chains stay short, probes stay tiny, and lookups remain honest O(1).
But once it climbs above the threshold, collisions pile up — this is the risk point that makes O(1) crawl.
Crossing the line triggers growth: allocate a bigger table so there are far more buckets than entries.
A bigger table alone isn't enough — every existing entry is rehashed and reinserted into the new buckets.
After rehash the load factor drops, chains fall back to about one, and average-case speed is restored.
The insight: load factor is a number you monitor and act on — resize on the threshold to keep the average case average.

collisions-load-factor.title: Predict the resize schedule
collisions-load-factor.summary: The worked example built a self-resizing map. Here you compute its resize SCHEDULE ahead of time: for a run of inserts, at which insert count each doubling fires, the final bucket count, and the load factor you land on. The growth policy, made predictable.
collisions-load-factor.starter:
def resize_schedule(num_inserts, start_buckets, max_load):
    buckets = start_buckets
    n = 0
    events = []
    # insert one at a time; when load exceeds max_load, double and record (n, new_buckets)
    return buckets, events

final, events = resize_schedule(12, 4, 0.66)
print("final buckets:", final)
print("resize events:", events)
print("final load factor:", round(12 / final, 3))

designing-good-keys.proof: A custom key class with matching __hash__/__eq__ used in a set, proving two logically-equal instances deduplicate to one entry.
designing-good-keys.unlock: You can state the hash/eq contract: equal objects MUST have equal hashes, and explain what breaks when they do not.
designing-good-keys.outcome: Design hashable keys with a correct __hash__/__eq__ contract so custom objects behave right in dicts and sets, and avoid the equal-but-different-hash bug.
designing-good-keys.doNotClaim: Don't claim any object works as a dict key — only objects whose __hash__ and __eq__ agree and stay stable are safe keys; a mutable field in the hash silently corrupts the table.

designing-good-keys.text: A team keyed a cache on custom objects. Two logically-identical instances were treated as different keys because the class used default identity hashing — so the cache never hit and memory ballooned. The fix is the hash/eq contract. This lesson teaches you to design keys that a hash table can trust.

A hash table places an entry by hash(key) and confirms it by key == key. That means a custom object used as a key must implement BOTH __hash__ and __eq__ consistently. Pythons rule (from the data model) is strict: objects that compare equal must have the same hash. Break it and dicts/sets misbehave in ways that look like heisenbugs — missed lookups, phantom duplicates. This lesson closes Module 3 by making you the designer of the key, not just a user of the table, which matters any time you cache, dedupe, or index by a compound identity.

designing-good-keys.prompt: Before reading: you define __eq__ on a class so two instances with the same id compare equal, but you do not define __hash__. What happens when you put them in a set?
designing-good-keys.reveal: Defining __eq__ without __hash__ makes the class UNHASHABLE in Python (the default __hash__ is set to None), so adding an instance to a set raises TypeError. If instead you kept the default identity __hash__ while overriding __eq__, you would violate the contract: two "equal" instances would have DIFFERENT hashes, land in different buckets, and both be stored — the set would hold duplicates and lookups would miss. You must define __hash__ to agree with __eq__.

designing-good-keys.intro: Base equality and hash on the same immutable identity fields so equal objects share a hash and dedupe correctly.
steps: __eq__ defines when two instances are "the same key" — here, same (x, y).
__hash__ must be built from the SAME fields used in __eq__, so equal objects hash equally.
Hash on IMMUTABLE identity fields only; if a field can change, the hash changes and the table breaks.
With the contract satisfied, equal instances share a bucket and dedupe to one entry.
designing-good-keys.commonMistake: Overriding __eq__ but leaving __hash__ as the default identity hash (or hashing different fields than __eq__ compares). Then two equal objects get different hashes, so a dict/set stores both and lookups for one may miss the other — the table silently violates its own uniqueness.

designing-good-keys.text: A hash table trusts two methods on every key: __hash__ (which bucket) and __eq__ (is this the same key). Designing a key means honoring the contract Python states in its data model: (1) if a == b then hash(a) == hash(b) — equal objects MUST have equal hashes, because they must land in the same bucket to be found; the converse need not hold (a hash collision between non-equal keys is fine, __eq__ disambiguates). (2) An objects hash MUST NOT change while it is in a table — so base the hash only on IMMUTABLE identity fields, never on a field you mutate, or the entry becomes unfindable (it now hashes to a different bucket than where it was placed). (3) In Python, defining __eq__ without __hash__ sets __hash__ to None, making the class unhashable on purpose — you must define both together. The practical recipe: pick the fields that define identity, use them in __eq__ (usually as a tuple comparison), and return hash(that_same_tuple) from __hash__. This is why immutable value types (tuples, frozenset, namedtuples, frozen dataclasses) make ideal keys and mutable objects make dangerous ones. Get the contract right and dedup, caching, and indexing "just work"; get it wrong and you get phantom duplicates and missed lookups that are miserable to debug.

storyboard.say: A hash table starts with a custom key object — to be trusted as a key, it must implement both __hash__ and __eq__ correctly.
__hash__ reads the object's immutable identity fields and computes which bucket the entry belongs in.
Inside that bucket, __eq__ runs to confirm identity — a hash picks the bucket, but == decides if it's truly the same key.
When == returns equal, the entries merge into one — that's dedup working: logically-identical keys collapse to a single entry.
But default identity hashing gives two equal objects different hashes, sending them to different buckets — a phantom duplicate.
The contract: if a equals b, their hashes must match, and the hash must never change while the key sits in the table.
Design keys on immutable identity fields and honor hash-eq consistency — that's how a hash table can trust your key.

binary-trees-traversal.proof: A binary tree whose three traversals are printed as computed value sequences, showing each order is genuinely different.
binary-trees-traversal.unlock: You can define a binary tree by its node structure and explain the difference between the three depth-first traversal orders.
binary-trees-traversal.outcome: Build a binary tree of nodes and traverse it three ways (pre-order, in-order, post-order), explaining what order each visit produces and when you use it.
binary-trees-traversal.doNotClaim: Don't claim traversal order does not matter — in-order on a BST yields sorted output, post-order safely frees children before parents; picking the wrong order silently produces wrong results.

binary-trees-traversal.text: A serializer walked a tree in the wrong order and produced output that could not be reconstructed, and a cleanup routine freed a parent before its children and corrupted state. Both were traversal-order bugs. Trees are everywhere — file systems, ASTs, the DOM — and knowing the three orders is how you walk them correctly. This lesson builds the tree and all three walks.

A binary tree is a hierarchy where each node has up to two children (left and right). It generalizes the linear structures into branching ones and is the substrate for BSTs, heaps, tries, expression trees, and parse trees. The core skill is TRAVERSAL — visiting every node in a defined order. Depth-first traversal has three flavors distinguished by WHEN you visit the node relative to its children: pre-order (node first), in-order (node between children), post-order (node last). Each order serves a purpose, and the rest of Module 4 assumes you can walk a tree.

binary-trees-traversal.prompt: Before reading: for a tree with root 2, left child 1, right child 3, what does pre-order, in-order, and post-order each print?
binary-trees-traversal.reveal: Pre-order (node, left, right): 2, 1, 3. In-order (left, node, right): 1, 2, 3. Post-order (left, right, node): 1, 3, 2. In-order gives sorted output here because this is a valid BST arrangement. The only difference between the three is WHEN the node itself is emitted relative to recursing into its subtrees — and that timing changes the whole sequence.

binary-trees-traversal.code:
class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, value, left=None, right=None):
        self.value = value
        self.left = left
        self.right = right

def pre_order(node, out):
    if node is None: return
    out.append(node.value)        # NODE first
    pre_order(node.left, out)
    pre_order(node.right, out)

def in_order(node, out):
    if node is None: return
    in_order(node.left, out)
    out.append(node.value)        # NODE between children
    in_order(node.right, out)

def post_order(node, out):
    if node is None: return
    post_order(node.left, out)
    post_order(node.right, out)
    out.append(node.value)        # NODE last
binary-trees-traversal.intro: A node holds a value and left/right child references. Each traversal is a recursion that differs only in where it emits the node.
steps: Each node has a value and up to two children; None marks an absent child (the base case of the recursion).
Pre-order emits the node BEFORE recursing — good for copying/serializing structure top-down.
In-order emits the node BETWEEN left and right — on a BST this yields sorted order.
Post-order emits the node AFTER both children — good for freeing/evaluating bottom-up.
binary-trees-traversal.commonMistake: Forgetting the base case `if node is None: return`, so the recursion dereferences a None child and crashes (AttributeError). Every traversal must stop at the empty subtree; that None check is the recursions floor.

binary-trees-traversal.text: A binary tree is built from nodes, each holding a value and references to a left and a right child (either of which may be absent). One node is the ROOT; nodes with no children are LEAVES; the number of edges on the longest root-to-leaf path is the HEIGHT. Traversal means visiting every node exactly once in some order, and the fundamental family is DEPTH-FIRST, which recurses fully into one subtree before the other. Its three variants differ by a single decision — WHEN to emit the current node relative to its children: PRE-ORDER (node, then left subtree, then right) captures structure top-down and is how you serialize or copy a tree; IN-ORDER (left, node, right) visits nodes in a left-to-right sweep, which on a binary SEARCH tree produces the values in SORTED order — a fact the next lesson depends on; POST-ORDER (left, right, node) finishes both children before the parent, which is what you need to evaluate an expression tree or free/delete a tree safely (children before parents). Each recursion has the same shape and the same base case (stop at an empty subtree); only the placement of the emit line changes. There is also breadth-first traversal (level by level), which uses a queue and reappears as BFS in Module 5. Choosing the order is not cosmetic: the wrong one yields unsorted output, unreconstructable serializations, or use-after-free bugs.

Emit between the subtrees — left, node, right — in-order. On a binary search tree this yields the values in sorted sequence.
Emit the node last — left, right, then node — post-order. Children are fully handled before the parent, safe for freeing or deletion.
Same tree, same recursion — only the emit point moves. Pick pre to serialize, in to sort, post to free, and both bugs disappear.

binary-search-trees.text: A team built a BST index and it was fast in testing and pathologically slow in production. The cause: production inserted keys in sorted order, so the "tree" degenerated into a one-sided chain — every search O(n). A BST is only as fast as it is balanced. This lesson builds the BST, proves the O(h) cost, and shows the degenerate case that motivates balanced trees.

A binary search tree adds an ORDERING INVARIANT to the binary tree: for every node, all values in its left subtree are smaller and all in its right subtree are larger. That invariant turns the tree into a searchable index — you descend left or right by comparison, halving the search space at each step WHEN the tree is balanced. BSTs (and their balanced variants) back ordered maps, range queries, and databases. This lesson also exposes the fatal weakness — height depends on insertion order — which is exactly why self-balancing trees exist.

binary-search-trees.prompt: Before reading: you insert 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 into an empty BST IN THAT ORDER. What shape does the tree take, and what is the cost of searching for 5?
binary-search-trees.reveal: Each new value is larger than all before it, so it goes to the right every time: the tree becomes a right-leaning chain 1->2->3->4->5 with height 4 — a linked list. Searching for 5 walks all the way down: O(n). This is the DEGENERATE BST. The invariant is intact, but with no balancing, sorted input destroys the O(log n) you wanted; height, not node count, is what O(h) charges.

binary-search-trees.intro: Insert by descending left/right on comparison until you find an empty slot; the same descent is how you search.
steps: The invariant left < node < right holds at EVERY node, not just the root.
Insert descends left or right by comparison until it hits an empty slot, then attaches the node.
Search follows the same left/right descent, discarding half the remaining tree at each balanced step.
Cost is O(height): ~log n if balanced, but n if the tree degenerated into a chain.
binary-search-trees.commonMistake: Assuming a BST stays balanced on its own. It does not — insertion order determines shape, and sorted or nearly-sorted inserts produce a linear chain with O(n) operations. A plain BST has no rebalancing; that guarantee requires a self-balancing variant.

binary-search-trees.text: A binary search tree maintains one invariant at every node: all keys in the left subtree are less than the node, and all keys in the right subtree are greater. That local rule creates a global order, which is why an IN-ORDER traversal emits the keys sorted (previous lesson) and why search is a guided descent: compare the target to the node, go left if smaller or right if larger, and each step discards an entire subtree. Insert works the same way — descend until you reach an empty slot and attach there. The cost of search, insert, and delete is O(h) where h is the HEIGHT of the tree, because that descent is at most one node per level. Here is the crux: h is NOT automatically log n. In a BALANCED tree (each nodes two subtrees roughly equal height) h = O(log n), so operations are O(log n) — the win that makes BSTs useful for ordered maps and range queries. But h depends on INSERTION ORDER. Insert already-sorted keys and every insertion goes the same direction, producing a degenerate chain of height n-1 — a linked list wearing a tree costume, with O(n) operations. So "BST is O(log n)" is really "O(h), which is O(log n) only if balanced." This gap is the entire reason self-balancing trees (AVL, red-black) exist: they perform rotations on insert/delete to keep h = O(log n) regardless of input order, trading a little bookkeeping for a worst-case guarantee. CPython does not ship a built-in balanced tree; when you need ordered operations you reach for the sortedcontainers library or keep data sorted in a list with bisect.

heaps-priority-queues.text: A scheduler needed "always give me the highest-priority task next" and used a list it re-sorted on every insert — O(n log n) per task. A heap does the same job in O(log n) per push and pop, because it maintains just enough order to know the extreme, not full sorted order. This lesson builds that intuition and uses Pythons heapq.

A binary heap is a COMPLETE binary tree (filled level by level, left to right) with the HEAP PROPERTY: every parent is <= its children (min-heap) or >= them (max-heap). That partial order is exactly enough to make the extreme element sit at the root in O(1), while push and pop cost only O(log n). Because the tree is complete, it needs no pointers: it packs into an array where node i has children at 2i+1 and 2i+2 and parent at (i-1)//2. Heaps power priority queues, Dijkstras algorithm, scheduling, and top-k selection. Python ships heapq (a min-heap) for exactly this.

heaps-priority-queues.prompt: Before reading: a heap keeps the smallest element at the top in O(1). Does that mean the heap array is sorted? If you pop repeatedly, in what order do elements come out?
heaps-priority-queues.reveal: No — a heap is only PARTIALLY ordered: each parent <= its children, so the MINIMUM is at the root, but siblings and cousins are unordered, and the raw array is not sorted. However, repeatedly POPPING (each pop removes the min and re-heapifies) yields elements in ascending sorted order — that is heapsort. The heap gives you the extreme cheaply and full sorted order only if you drain it, each pop O(log n).

heaps-priority-queues.code:
import heapq

# heapq maintains a min-heap invariant on a plain list:
#   heap[k] <= heap[2k+1] and heap[k] <= heap[2k+2]
tasks = []
heapq.heappush(tasks, (3, "email"))     # (priority, item); O(log n) sift-up
heapq.heappush(tasks, (1, "pager"))
heapq.heappush(tasks, (2, "ticket"))

# heap[0] is always the minimum-priority tuple: O(1) to read
first = tasks[0]                        # (1, "pager")

# popping repeatedly yields ascending priority order, each pop O(log n):
order = [heapq.heappop(tasks) for _ in range(len(tasks))]
heaps-priority-queues.intro: A complete tree in an array: parent/child by index arithmetic. Push then sift up; pop the root, move the last element up, then sift down.
steps: A complete tree packs into an array; node i has children 2i+1, 2i+2 and parent (i-1)//2 — no pointers needed.
The heap property (parent <= children) keeps the minimum at index 0, readable in O(1).
Push appends then SIFTS UP (swap with parent while smaller): O(log n), the tree height.
Pop removes the root, moves the last element to the top, and SIFTS DOWN to restore the property: O(log n).
heaps-priority-queues.commonMistake: Treating the heap array as sorted — e.g. reading heap[1] as the second-smallest. Only heap[0] is guaranteed (the min); the rest is partially ordered. To get sorted order you must POP repeatedly (heapsort) or use sorted(), not index into the raw heap.

heaps-priority-queues.text: A binary heap is a COMPLETE binary tree (every level full except possibly the last, which fills left to right) obeying the HEAP PROPERTY: in a min-heap every parent key is <= both its children (max-heap: >=). Two consequences make it the priority-queue structure. First, completeness means the tree has no gaps, so it needs NO pointers — it lives in a flat array where the node at index i has its children at 2i+1 and 2i+2 and its parent at (i-1)//2. This index arithmetic replaces child references and gives perfect cache locality (contiguous storage) on top of the algorithmic win. Second, the heap property is a PARTIAL order — it constrains parent vs child but says nothing about siblings — which is exactly enough to guarantee the extreme (min or max) sits at the root, readable in O(1), without paying to fully sort. Maintaining the property costs O(log n): a PUSH appends at the end and SIFTS UP (repeatedly swaps with its parent while it violates the order); a POP removes the root, moves the last element into the root slot, and SIFTS DOWN (swaps with the smaller child while it violates the order). Both walk at most the trees height, which is log n because the tree is complete. Building a heap from n items is O(n) (heapify), better than n pushes. The key mental correction: a heap is NOT sorted; heap[0] is the min, the rest is only partially ordered, and full sorted order comes only from draining it (each pop O(log n), total O(n log n) — heapsort). Pythons heapq operates a min-heap directly on a list; for a max-heap, negate the keys or use a wrapper.

That is the insight: maintain just enough order to know the extreme in O(1), so push and pop cost O(log n), not a re-sort.

tries.text: An autocomplete feature scanned every stored term to find prefix matches — O(number_of_words * length) per keystroke, unusable at scale. A trie answers "all words starting with X" by walking X once, in O(length of X). This lesson builds the trie and shows why prefix work is where it shines.

A trie (prefix tree) is a tree keyed by the CHARACTERS of strings: each edge is a character, each root-to-node path spells a prefix, and a marked node means "a word ends here." Because common prefixes share the same path, the trie is the natural structure for autocomplete, spell-check, IP routing tables, and dictionary lookups. Its defining property: operations cost O(L) in the key length, independent of the number of stored keys N — a different scaling axis from the hash maps average O(1)-per-op-but-hash-the-whole-key model. This closes the trees module with a tree specialized for strings.

tries.reveal: The prefix "car" is stored ONCE as a shared path c->a->r; "cart" and "care" branch off the r node. Checking "cart" walks c->a->r->t, four steps — O(L) where L=4, the length of the query — regardless of how many total words the trie holds. Shared prefixes save both space and time, and cost scales with word length, not word count.

steps: Each node holds a char->child map and an is_word flag; the ROOT represents the empty prefix.
Insert walks the characters, creating missing child nodes, then marks the final node as a word end — O(L).
Exact-word search walks the path AND checks is_word (so "car" is not "found" if only "cart" was inserted).
Prefix search only needs the path to exist — that is the autocomplete primitive, also O(L).

tries.text: A trie stores a set of strings as paths in a tree whose edges are characters. Starting from a root that stands for the empty prefix, each character of a key selects (or creates) a child, so the path spelled from the root to a node IS a prefix, and a boolean flag on a node marks "a complete word ends here." The structural payoff is PREFIX SHARING: "car," "cart," and "care" all reuse the single path c->a->r, then branch — saving space when keys overlap and making prefix questions trivial. Operations cost O(L) where L is the length of the key or query: insert and exact-match search each take one step per character, and crucially this is INDEPENDENT of N, the number of stored keys — a trie with a million words checks a 5-character word in 5 steps. That is a genuinely different scaling story from a hash map, whose per-operation cost is average O(1) but which must hash the whole key (also ~O(L)) and, decisively, CANNOT answer "give me every key with prefix X" without scanning — the trie does it by walking X once and then enumerating the subtree below. The costs: a trie spends a node (and a small map) per distinct prefix character, so it uses more memory than a hash set for keys with little shared structure, and it is specialized to sequences (strings, sequences of tokens). Use a trie when prefix queries, autocomplete, longest-prefix matching (routing), or ordered/shared-prefix iteration matter; use a hash set/map when you only need exact membership and want minimal memory.

graph-representations.text: A social graph with millions of users and a handful of friends each was stored as a full adjacency matrix — a V-by-V grid that was 99.9% empty and blew the memory budget. An adjacency list stores only the edges that exist. The representation is a real design decision driven by density. This lesson builds both and shows the tradeoff.

A graph is a set of VERTICES connected by EDGES (directed or undirected, optionally weighted) — the model for networks, maps, dependencies, and the web. Before you can traverse or search a graph you must STORE it, and there are two canonical layouts: the ADJACENCY LIST (each vertex maps to its neighbors) and the ADJACENCY MATRIX (a V-by-V grid where cell [u][v] marks an edge). They differ in space and in which queries are cheap, and the deciding factor is DENSITY (how many of the possible edges exist). This lesson sets up BFS/DFS next, which run on top of whichever representation you choose.

graph-representations.prompt: Before reading: a graph has 1,000,000 vertices but each vertex has only ~10 edges. How much space does an adjacency matrix use vs an adjacency list, and which fits in memory?
graph-representations.reveal: A matrix is V-by-V = 10^12 cells regardless of how few edges exist — hopeless. An adjacency list stores only real edges: ~V + E = 10^6 + 10^7 = ~1.1 * 10^7 entries — five orders of magnitude smaller and easily in memory. For this SPARSE graph the adjacency list is the only viable choice; the matrix would only make sense if nearly every pair were connected (a dense graph).
