graph-representations.intro: Adjacency list: dict of vertex -> neighbor set (O(V+E) space). Adjacency matrix: V-by-V grid (O(V^2) space, O(1) edge test).
steps: An adjacency list maps each vertex to its set/list of neighbors, storing only real edges: O(V+E) space.
Getting a vertexs neighbors from the list is O(degree) — exactly the edges you need to visit.
An adjacency matrix is a V-by-V grid with a 1 where an edge exists: O(V^2) space no matter how sparse.
A matrix answers "is there an edge u-v?" in O(1) by indexing matrix[u][v]; the list needs an O(degree) check.
graph-representations.commonMistake: Using an adjacency matrix for a large sparse graph. The V^2 space is dominated by zeros (absent edges) and wastes memory that scales with the SQUARE of vertices; for sparse graphs the adjacency lists O(V+E) is dramatically smaller and neighbor scans are faster too.

graph-representations.text: A graph of V vertices and E edges can be stored two ways, and the right one depends on DENSITY = E relative to the maximum V^2. The ADJACENCY LIST maps each vertex to a collection of its neighbors (a dict of sets, or list of lists). It uses O(V + E) space — proportional to what actually exists — and getting a vertexs neighbors is O(1) to reach the collection plus O(degree) to iterate it, which is exactly the work a traversal needs. Its weakness: testing whether a SPECIFIC edge u-v exists means scanning us neighbors, O(degree). The ADJACENCY MATRIX is a V-by-V grid where cell [u][v] is 1 if the edge exists. It uses O(V^2) space regardless of how few edges there are, but it answers "does edge u-v exist?" in O(1) by direct indexing and stores edge WEIGHTS naturally in the cell. The decision: for SPARSE graphs (E much less than V^2 — social networks, road maps, dependency graphs, most real graphs), the adjacency list wins decisively on memory and gives cache-reasonable neighbor iteration; for DENSE graphs (E approaching V^2) or workloads dominated by random edge-existence/weight lookups, the matrix wins on those O(1) queries and its simplicity. Directedness and weights layer onto either: a directed edge sets only [u][v] (not [v][u]); a weight replaces the 1 with the weight, or the neighbor set with (neighbor, weight) pairs. BFS and DFS (next lesson) run on either representation, but their O(V+E) runtime assumes the adjacency lists O(degree) neighbor access — a matrix makes traversal O(V^2) because each vertex scans a full row.
graph-representations.title: List vs matrix is a density decision: O(V+E) sparse storage vs O(V^2) with O(1) edge tests
Adjacency list vs adjacency matrix
graph-representations.subtitle: sparse -> list (O(V+E)); dense / edge-tests -> matrix (O(V^2), O(1) test)

The lesson: a million-user social graph is sparse, so a matrix was 99.9% empty. Density is a real design decision, not a default.

bfs-dfs.text: A "find the shortest referral chain between two users" feature used DFS and returned wildly long chains, and a crawler without a visited set looped forever on a cycle. Both are traversal bugs: DFS is the wrong tool for shortest paths, and skipping visited-tracking breaks on cycles. This lesson builds both searches correctly and shows exactly what each guarantees.

Graph SEARCH visits vertices reachable from a start, and the two fundamental strategies differ only in the ORDER they explore, set by the data structure holding the frontier. BFS uses a FIFO QUEUE (the deque from Module 2) and explores in rings of increasing distance, which makes it find the shortest path in an UNWEIGHTED graph. DFS uses a STACK (or recursion, the call stack from Module 2) and plunges down one path before backtracking. Both need a VISITED SET (the O(1) membership from Module 3) to avoid revisiting nodes and to terminate on cycles. Together they underlie connectivity, shortest paths, cycle detection, and topological sort — and they assemble the structures from the whole course.

bfs-dfs.prompt: Before reading: BFS uses a queue and DFS uses a stack. Which one finds the fewest-edges path between two nodes in an unweighted graph, and why?
bfs-dfs.reveal: BFS. A FIFO queue processes all vertices at distance 1 before any at distance 2, then all at distance 2 before distance 3 — it expands in rings of increasing distance. So the FIRST time BFS reaches a target, it is via a fewest-edges path. DFS uses a stack and dives deep down one branch first, so it may reach the target by a long, winding route before a short one exists — it finds A path, not the shortest.

bfs-dfs.intro: BFS with a deque explores level by level and records distances; DFS with recursion goes deep. Both mark visited on discovery.
steps: BFS uses a FIFO queue: it drains distance-1 nodes before distance-2, so first-arrival = shortest unweighted path.
DFS uses a stack (here the recursion/call stack): it follows one branch to the end before backtracking.
Both add a node to VISITED the moment they discover it — never after, or a node can be queued/recursed twice.
The visited set makes each vertex and edge processed once: O(V+E), and it is what stops cycles from looping forever.
bfs-dfs.commonMistake: Marking a node visited when you POP it instead of when you DISCOVER (enqueue) it. Then the same node can be enqueued multiple times before it is first popped, inflating work and, on cycles, risking nontermination. Mark visited at the moment you add to the frontier.

bfs-dfs.text: BFS and DFS both visit every vertex reachable from a start, processing each vertex and edge once for O(V+E) time on an adjacency list — but they explore in opposite orders, and the order is dictated entirely by the structure holding the FRONTIER (the discovered-but-not-yet-expanded vertices). BFS uses a FIFO QUEUE: it fully expands all vertices at distance d before any at distance d+1, sweeping outward in concentric rings. That level-by-level order is why BFS finds the SHORTEST PATH (fewest edges) in an unweighted graph — the first time it reaches a vertex is necessarily by a minimum-edge route, and you can record dist[v] = dist[u] + 1 as you go. DFS uses a STACK (explicitly, or implicitly via recursion — the call stack from the stacks lesson): it dives down one branch as far as possible, then backtracks, which is ideal for exhaustively exploring, detecting cycles, and producing topological orders, but it finds SOME path, not the shortest. The non-negotiable shared ingredient is a VISITED SET: mark each vertex the moment it is DISCOVERED (added to the frontier), so (1) no vertex is processed twice — preserving O(V+E) — and (2) cycles terminate instead of looping forever. This lesson is the payoff of the whole course: BFS is a queue (Module 2) + a visited set (Module 3) over an adjacency list (Module 5); DFS is a stack + the same set. Weighted shortest paths need Dijkstra, which swaps the plain queue for the priority queue/heap from Module 4 — same skeleton, smarter frontier.

storyboard.say: Every graph search starts at one vertex and explores outward, but the frontier structure it feeds into decides the entire exploration order.
Send the start into a FIFO queue and you get BFS: popleft always pulls the oldest-discovered vertex, sweeping outward in rings of equal distance.
Because BFS expands all vertices at distance d before any at d+1, the first time it reaches a node is by fewest edges, giving the shortest path.
Feed the same start into a stack and you get DFS: pop or recurse dives down one path as deep as it can, then backtracks.
This is the referral-chain bug: DFS returns a path, not the shortest one, so it happily reported wildly long chains between users.
Both BFS and DFS mark each vertex in the visited set the moment they discover it, so no vertex is ever expanded twice.
The visited set is what makes traversal O(V+E) and stops cycles from looping forever, exactly the crawler bug from skipping it.

BFS runs by recursion while DFS runs off a queue, and recursion naturally reaches nearer vertices before the farther ones.
bfs-dfs.question: Why does BFS find the shortest path (fewest edges) in an unweighted graph while DFS does not?

The moment BFS first reaches a vertex, no shorter (fewer-edge) route to it exists, so recorded distances are shortest. DFS uses a stack and follows one branch to its end before others, so it may discover a vertex via a long path — it finds a path, not the shortest.

choosing-the-structure.proof: A decision function that maps a requirements profile to a recommended structure and prints the pick for several real workloads.
choosing-the-structure.unlock: You can drive from the QUESTION your data must answer to the structure whose strengths match — across the whole course catalog.
choosing-the-structure.outcome: Turn a set of access requirements (lookup by key? ordered? prefix? priority? relationships?) into a data-structure choice with a repeatable decision procedure, not a guess.
choosing-the-structure.doNotClaim: Don't claim there is one best data structure — the best one is defined by the operations you need cheap; the skill is reading requirements into the catalog, not memorizing a favorite.

choosing-the-structure.text: A design doc said "use a list" for everything, and three features later the team was fighting O(n) lookups, missing prefix search, and manual priority sorting. Each was a structure chosen by habit, not by the question the data had to answer. This lesson gives you a decision procedure that maps requirements to the right structure across everything you have learned.

This lesson synthesizes the course. Every structure you have built answers a particular QUESTION cheaply: a hash map answers "value for this exact key?" in O(1); a BST/sorted structure answers "keys in a range / in order?"; a trie answers "keys with this prefix?"; a heap answers "the current extreme?"; a graph answers "what is connected to what?"; a list/array answers "the element at this index?" and "append at the end." Choosing well means reading your requirements — which operations, how often, ordered or not — and matching them to the structure whose strengths fit. That decision procedure is the reusable output of the whole course and the setup for the capstone.

choosing-the-structure.prompt: Before reading: you need (a) exact lookup by user id, (b) autocomplete on usernames, and (c) always serve the highest-priority pending job. Which structure for each?
choosing-the-structure.reveal: (a) Exact lookup by key -> a HASH MAP (dict): average O(1) get by id. (b) Prefix/autocomplete on strings -> a TRIE: O(L) prefix queries a hash map cannot do. (c) Repeatedly get the extreme -> a HEAP / priority queue: O(log n) push/pop with the top in O(1). Three different questions, three different structures — the decision comes from the OPERATION you need cheap, not from one all-purpose container.

choosing-the-structure.code:
def choose(req):
    # req flags describe what the data must answer cheaply
    if req.get("relationships"):         return "graph"          # connections between entities
    if req.get("prefix"):                return "trie"           # autocomplete / longest-prefix
    if req.get("repeated_extreme"):      return "heap"           # always the min/max next
    if req.get("ordered") or req.get("range"): return "balanced tree / sorted list"
    if req.get("key_lookup"):            return "hash map (dict)" # exact key -> value, O(1)
    if req.get("unique"):                return "set"            # membership / dedup
    return "list / array"                                        # index + end-append

profiles = {
    "user store":   {"key_lookup": True},
    "autocomplete": {"prefix": True},
    "scheduler":    {"repeated_extreme": True},
    "leaderboard":  {"ordered": True, "range": True},
    "social graph": {"relationships": True},
}
choosing-the-structure.intro: Encode the decision as questions in priority order: relationships -> graph; prefix -> trie; extreme-repeatedly -> heap; ordered/range -> tree/sorted; exact-key -> hash map; else index/append -> list.
steps: Start from the QUESTION the data must answer cheaply, not from a default container.
Relationships between entities -> a graph; prefix/autocomplete -> a trie.
Repeatedly needing the extreme -> a heap; ordered iteration or range queries -> a balanced tree or sorted list.
Exact key -> value -> a hash map; membership/dedup -> a set; plain indexed sequence -> a list.
choosing-the-structure.commonMistake: Defaulting to a list for everything because it is the most familiar. A list is only right for indexed access and end-append; using it for key lookup (O(n)), priority (manual re-sort), or prefix search (full scan) reintroduces exactly the O(n)/O(n^2) problems the specialized structures were built to avoid.

choosing-the-structure.text: There is no universally best data structure — each one is a specialist that makes a particular QUESTION cheap and other questions expensive, so choosing is a matter of reading your requirements against the catalog you have built. Work from the dominant operations. "Value for this EXACT key?" -> HASH MAP (dict): average O(1) get/put/delete, but unordered and no range/prefix. "Is this present / is it unique?" -> SET: O(1) membership and dedup. "Keys in ORDER or in a RANGE?" -> a balanced BST or a sorted list with bisect: O(log n) ordered queries the hash map cannot do. "Keys sharing a PREFIX (autocomplete)?" -> TRIE: O(L) prefix work independent of key count. "The current MIN/MAX, repeatedly?" -> HEAP / priority queue: O(log n) push/pop, O(1) peek. "RELATIONSHIPS between entities / reachability / shortest path?" -> GRAPH with BFS/DFS. "Element at an INDEX, or append at the end, cache-friendly scans?" -> LIST/ARRAY: O(1) index and amortized O(1) append. "Add/remove at the FRONT (or both ends)?" -> DEQUE. Secondary factors break ties: memory budget (matrix vs list, trie vs set), locality (contiguous arrays beat pointer structures when you scan), and worst-case guarantees (balanced tree vs plain BST). The procedure is: (1) list the operations and their frequencies, (2) identify the one or two that dominate, (3) pick the structure whose strengths cover them, (4) confirm the rest are acceptable, (5) break ties on memory/locality. That is the whole engineering value of this course — not memorizing Big-O tables, but mapping a real requirement to the structure that answers it cheaply.

storyboard.say: Every structure choice starts here: read the requirements first, and ask what dominant question the data actually has to answer.
First branch: are entities connected to each other? If relationships dominate, you need a graph — connectivity is what it makes cheap.
No graph? Ask the specialist question: do you need prefix search, the running extreme, or ordered range queries?
Yes to any of those routes to a specialist: a trie for prefixes, a heap for the current min or max, a sorted tree for order.
If none of those apply, drop to the workhorse question: do you look things up by an exact, unique key?
Yes — exact key lookup — means a hash map or set: average O(1) get, put, and membership tests.
No exact-key need? A list or deque is the default, cheap only at an index or at the ends.
The insight: no structure is best — each is a specialist, so let the dominant question, not habit, pick it.

optionA.text: A dict for O(1) exact lookup plus a sorted structure for range queries. Each op is optimal, at the cost of extra memory and keeping the two in sync on writes.
optionA.label: Two structures (hash map + sorted index)

optionB.text: A single balanced tree / sorted container gives O(log n) BOTH for exact lookup and range — one structure, no sync — but exact lookup is O(log n) instead of the hash maps O(1).
optionB.label: One ordered structure

choosing-the-structure.guidance: If exact lookups are extremely hot and ranges are secondary, maintain both (A): pay the memory and sync cost to get O(1) on the dominant op. If the mix is balanced or writes are frequent (making two-structure sync painful), a single ordered structure (B) is simpler and its O(log n) lookup is usually fine. Decide by which operation dominates and how costly keeping two structures consistent would be.
choosing-the-structure.question: A workload needs BOTH exact key lookup AND ordered range queries. One structure or two?

options: A trie, because it answers prefix queries in O(L) — something a hash set cannot do without scanning every stored key.
A plain list, because you can scan it front to back and collect every key that happens to start with the given prefix.
A hash set, because its O(1) membership also covers prefix lookups by hashing each prefix directly to its own bucket.
A heap, because it keeps entries ordered, so all keys sharing a prefix sit together and are cheap to enumerate in turn.
choosing-the-structure.question: You need autocomplete (all terms starting with a prefix) AND exact membership. What is the right primary structure for the autocomplete part?
choosing-the-structure.explanation: Prefix/autocomplete is the tries defining strength: walk the prefix in O(L) and enumerate the subtree below. A hash set gives O(1) EXACT membership but has no notion of prefixes, so finding all keys with a prefix would require scanning every key. Match the structure to the question — prefix -> trie — and you can keep a set alongside for exact membership if needed.

This capstone runs the whole course loop on one problem. The feature has two distinct questions — "who are the top k?" (a repeated-extreme / partial-order query -> a heap) and "what is X's score?" (exact key lookup -> a hash map) — and no single structure answers both cheaply. The right design composes two: a dict for O(1) lookup and a heap for O(k log n) top-k selection. You will read the requirements, pick the structures with the Module 5 decision procedure, implement them, and PROVE the result with computed output. This is the "pick + implement the structure a feature needs" deliverable the blueprint calls for.

capstone-pick-and-implement.prompt: Before reading: a leaderboard must return the top 3 scores AND look up any players score by name in O(1). Can one structure do both well? What combination would you use?
capstone-pick-and-implement.reveal: No single structure is optimal for both. A hash map gives O(1) name->score lookup but has no notion of "top" (finding the max is O(n)). A heap gives you the extreme cheaply but cannot look up an arbitrary name. The right answer is to COMPOSE: a dict for O(1) exact lookup plus a heap (or heapq.nlargest) for top-k. Each structure answers the question it is best at; together they cover the spec.

capstone-pick-and-implement.intro: Compose a hash map (name->score) for exact lookup with a heap-based top-k selection; each structure serves the query it is best at.
steps: Requirement 1 (exact lookup by name) -> a hash map: dict.get is average O(1).
Requirement 2 (top-k by score) -> a heap: heapq.nlargest selects the k largest in O(n log k).
Neither structure alone covers both, so the design COMPOSES them — the course lesson in one build.
Prove it with computed output: the actual top-3 list and a real O(1) lookup, not a hardcoded demo.
capstone-pick-and-implement.commonMistake: Forcing one structure to do both jobs — e.g. keeping only a sorted list, which makes top-k trivial but every score update an O(n) re-sort/insert, or keeping only a dict and scanning all n entries for the top each time. The whole point is to compose the right structure per question.

capstone-pick-and-implement.text: The capstone is the course thesis made concrete: a real feature usually poses MORE THAN ONE question, and the engineering move is to choose the right structure for EACH and compose them, rather than bending one structure to do everything. The leaderboard poses two questions with different optimal answers. "What is player X's score?" is exact key lookup -> a HASH MAP (dict), average O(1), the structure from Module 3. "Who are the top k by score?" is a partial-order / repeated-extreme query -> a HEAP, where heapq.nlargest returns the k largest in O(n log k) (and a maintained heap gives O(log n) incremental updates), the structure from Module 4. Compose them and both requirements are met at the right complexity; try to use only a dict and top-k becomes an O(n) scan each call; use only a sorted list and every score update is an O(n) shift. The full loop you now own: (1) FRAME the feature as a set of questions/operations; (2) ROUTE each to a structure via the decision procedure; (3) MAP the design (which structure answers which query, and how they share data); (4) DECIDE under constraints (memory, update frequency, whether to precompute); (5) PROVE it with a COMPUTED result — here, the actual top-3 and a real lookup, both printed from the running structures, not asserted. That final step — proof, not vibes — is what separates a finished data-structure choice from a hopeful one, and it is the standard every lesson in this course has been training.

storyboard.say: The capstone spec asks for one feature that must answer two very different questions at once.
Reaching for a single structure fails: one of the two operations always collapses to slow O(n).
So we route each question separately: exact name lookups go to a hash map keyed by player name.
The other question, who are the top players, is routed to a heap that ranks by score.
The map does what it is best at: score_of(name) is an average O(1) get, instant by key.
The heap does what it is best at: nlargest selects the top three in O(n log k) partial order.
Both operations converge into one computed result, each proven by real output rather than claimed.
That is the course thesis made concrete: pick the right structure per question, then compose them.

capstone-pick-and-implement.task: Re-sorting the whole list on every update is O(n log n) per submit. Separate exact storage from top-k selection.
capstone-pick-and-implement.symptom: A leaderboard returns the correct top players but its throughput collapses as scores update frequently.

optionA.text: Store scores in a dict and call heapq.nlargest when asked: O(n log k) per query, zero maintenance on writes. Simple; wasteful if top-k is queried very frequently on a large, rarely-changing set.
optionA.label: Recompute on demand (nlargest)

optionB.text: Keep a heap or sorted index updated on each submit so top-k reads are O(k). Faster reads, but every write pays maintenance and you must keep it consistent with the dict.
optionB.label: Maintain a running structure

capstone-pick-and-implement.guidance: If reads dominate a large, slow-changing dataset, maintain a running structure (B) so hot top-k reads are cheap. If writes are frequent or the set is small, recompute on demand (A) — the O(n log k) query is fine and you avoid all maintenance/consistency cost. This is the same read-vs-write, precompute-vs-on-demand judgment the whole course has been building toward; decide by the query/update ratio.
